client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time there's a family get-together, I just... can't seem to enjoy it the way I used to, because her absence feels like this huge weight sitting on everyone, or at least on me. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a try.
therapist: It means a lot that you took this step, even when part of you wasn't sure it would help — that kind of courage deserves recognition. Losing your grandmother and then facing family gatherings without her sounds incredibly painful, like joy and grief are colliding in a way that feels impossible to navigate. I'm curious — when you're at one of those gatherings and the weight feels heaviest, what kinds of thoughts tend to run through your mind in those moments?

client: Mostly I keep thinking that we should be talking about her, laughing about old memories or something, but nobody really brings her up and it feels like we're all just pretending everything is normal. And then I start wondering if I'm the only one who's still this affected by it, which makes me feel kind of alone in the room even when I'm surrounded by family. There's also this guilt that creeps in whenever I do start to smile or laugh at something, like I'm somehow betraying her by having a good moment.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds so heavy — the loneliness of grieving in a room full of people, plus that guilt that swoops in the moment you catch a breath of joy. I want to gently offer another perspective on that guilt: is it possible that your grandmother, who was clearly so loved, would have *wanted* you to laugh and feel warmth with your family? It might be worth exploring — when you imagine her watching one of those moments where you smile, what do you think she would actually feel seeing that?

client: Honestly, I know in my head that she would have wanted us to be happy — she was that kind of person, always trying to make everyone laugh. But knowing that and actually feeling it in the moment are two completely different things, and when the guilt hits, that logical part of me just kind of shuts off. It's like I can't access that thought when I actually need it.
therapist: You've just identified something really important — that the knowledge is *there*, but grief has a way of making it unreachable exactly when you need it most, and that gap between knowing and feeling is one of the most human and frustrating parts of loss. In CBT, we sometimes create small "anchors" — like a written note, a photo, or even a phrase you prepare in advance — so that the logical, loving part of you has a way to break through in those overwhelming moments. Would you be open to thinking about what a small reminder like that might look like for you, something that feels true to who your grandmother actually was?

client: I guess I can see the logic in that, but I'm a little skeptical that carrying around a note or a photo is actually going to stop that guilt in its tracks when it hits. It feels almost too simple for something that feels this overwhelming, you know? Though I will say, she had this one saying she always used when any of us were being too hard on ourselves — something like "life is for the living" — and when you mentioned a phrase, that one kind of just came to me.
therapist: That phrase just surfaced naturally from somewhere deep and loving inside you, which tells me it already carries real weight — that's not a coincidence, that's her voice, and it's clearly still with you. Your skepticism is completely fair, and I'd never want to oversimplify something this painful; the goal isn't to erase the guilt instantly, but to give that wise part of you a fighting chance to be heard in the moment. I wonder — the next time you're at a gathering and you feel that guilt starting to creep in, what do you think it might feel like to quietly let her own words speak back to you?

client: I think it might actually feel comforting in a way, because it would be like she's still there in some small sense, which is kind of what I've been missing. But I'm also worried that in the middle of a noisy family gathering, with everyone around, I'm not going to have the mental space to even remember to try it — the guilt just kind of ambushes me before I can think straight. I suppose the real question is how I actually make that a reflex instead of something I have to consciously remember to do.
therapist: You've just moved from "will this work?" to "how do I make it work?" — that's a meaningful shift, and it shows you're already investing in this in a real way. Reflexes in our thinking are built through repetition in *lower-stakes* moments, so practicing her phrase when you're calm and safe — maybe even at home when you look at a photo of her — can help wire it in so it's more accessible when the ambush hits. I'm curious, are there small everyday moments, even outside of family gatherings, where that guilt or that sense of her absence shows up, where you might begin practicing letting her words in?

client: Yeah, it actually comes up a lot in quieter moments — like when I'm cooking something she used to make, or even just on Sunday mornings because that's when she would always call me. Those moments catch me off guard in a different way than the family gatherings, they're more private, but honestly they might be even harder because there's no distraction to pull me out of it. I can see how those could be the moments to practice, but I'm a little afraid that intentionally sitting with her memory like that, without any distraction, might just make the grief worse instead of better.
therapist: That fear makes complete sense — it's a very natural instinct to worry that leaning *into* the pain will overwhelm you, but what you're describing, those Sunday mornings and cooking moments, are actually grief reaching out for connection, not just loss. Gently sitting with her memory in those quiet spaces, with her phrase as a kind of companion, isn't about making yourself hurt more — it's about slowly teaching your heart that you can hold both the sadness *and* her love at the same time without being destroyed by it. What do you think it might feel like to try, just once, to let yourself stay in one of those moments — maybe while cooking something of hers — and see what happens when you invite her words in rather than reaching for a distraction?

client: I think it might actually be really emotional in a way I'm not sure I'm ready for, because those cooking moments already feel fragile and I worry about just breaking down completely in the middle of my kitchen with no one around. But there's also a small part of me that feels like maybe that's exactly what I've been avoiding, and avoiding it hasn't really made the Sunday mornings or the cooking any easier. I guess I could try it once with one of her simpler recipes, something that doesn't carry quite as much weight as the big ones she made for holidays.
therapist: That small, honest part of you that recognizes the avoidance hasn't been working — that's real wisdom, and it took courage to say it out loud. Choosing a simpler recipe is not taking the easy way out, it's actually a thoughtful, compassionate way to ease yourself into something tender rather than throwing yourself into the deep end, and that's exactly the right instinct. If you do find yourself breaking down in the kitchen, I want you to consider — might that actually be your grief finally getting the space it's been asking for, rather than something going wrong?

client: When you put it that way, breaking down doesn't sound quite as terrifying — it actually reframes it a little, like maybe crying in my kitchen isn't falling apart but more like finally letting something through that's been stuck. I think I've been treating grief like something to manage and contain, and the idea that it might just need space is... different from how I've been thinking about it. I'm still nervous, but I think I'm willing to try the recipe thing this week, maybe something like her simple shortbread cookies, and see what happens when I let her phrase be there with me instead of turning on the TV to drown it out.
therapist: The shift you just described — from grief as something to *contain* to grief as something that needs *space* — is genuinely significant, and the fact that you arrived at that yourself makes it all the more real and lasting. Shortbread cookies, her phrase, and no TV sounds like a quietly brave and beautiful way to spend some time with her this week. When you do try it, I'd love to hear what you notice — not just about the grief, but about whether there's anything else present in that kitchen alongside the sadness.

client: That question about what else might be present is something I hadn't even considered — I've been so focused on bracing for the sadness that I never thought there might be something else in the room, maybe something closer to gratitude or even warmth. I'll try to pay attention to that, though I'm honestly not sure I'll be in a headspace to notice much beyond the emotions hitting me. But I'll come back and tell you what happened, and I think just having something concrete to do and actually report back on makes this feel a little less like floating in the grief with no direction.
therapist: Having something to return to and share is itself a small act of hope, and I think that matters more than you might realize right now. You came in today unsure that talking would change anything, and you're leaving with her words, her recipe, and a little more curiosity about your own grief — that's a real shift in one conversation. Before you go, I'm wondering — is there anything you want to gently remind yourself of, or hold onto, for those moments this week when the nervousness about trying this starts to creep in?

client: I think what I want to hold onto is that avoiding it hasn't actually been protecting me — it's just been keeping me stuck, and I've been stuck for a month now. Her saying "life is for the living" feels like the right thing to come back to when the nervousness hits, because it's not my words telling me it's okay, it's hers. I'm still a little scared this won't go the way I'm hoping, but I think I came in today expecting nothing and somehow ended up with something, so maybe that's worth trusting a little.
therapist: What you just said — that you came in expecting nothing and found something — is itself a quiet example of what happens when we stop avoiding and let something in, which is exactly what you're about to practice with those cookies. Her words, your courage, and that hard-won insight about being stuck are real things you're carrying out of here today, and they belong to you. I'll be here when you come back, and I'm already rooting for you and those shortbread cookies.
